title: Why Does Pastoral Visitation Still Matter?
subtitle: On visitation, the hospital room, and the unscalable work that is most of the job

sections.title: The Work No One Applauds
sections.body:
You will not be known for this. The sermon gets the praise. The building campaign gets the photographs. The conference invitation comes because of the platform, not because of the afternoon you spent in a recliner across from a man who could not remember your name.

But the afternoon was the job. The sermon was the part of the job other people could see.

Most of ministry happens where no one is watching. A driveway at dusk. A waiting room with bad coffee. A kitchen table with the mail still unopened because grief has frozen the house in place. This is the unscalable work. You cannot delegate it, you cannot automate it, you cannot livestream it. You can only go. I have stood in pulpits and been thanked for words I labored over for twelve hours. I have sat in living rooms and said almost nothing, and that was the hour that mattered. I did not always believe that. I wanted the visible thing. I wanted to be useful in a way that showed.

Presence does not show. Presence is the part of the work only God and one suffering person will ever see.

sections.title: What the Body Already Knows
sections.body:
We are not souls renting bodies. We are creatures God made from dust and called good, and the incarnation is the proof that bodies matter to him. The Word did not send word. The Word became flesh and moved into the neighborhood, and the neighborhood was a real place with real dust on its roads.

So when you go to the hospital, you are not delivering a service. You are doing theology with your feet.

The phone call says I am thinking of you. The visit says I am here. Those are not the same sentence. A text can be sent from anywhere by anyone in any state of distraction. A body in a chair has made a decision that costs something. It costs the afternoon. It costs the drive. It costs the discomfort of not knowing what to say and saying it anyway. The widow remembers who came. She does not remember what they said, because mostly they said nothing worth remembering, but she remembers the chair pulled close and the hand that held hers while the machines beeped. I have forgotten a thousand of my own sentences. I have never forgotten who showed up when my father was dying and who did not.

sections.title: The Hospital Room
sections.body:
Here is the practical shape of it, because vague encouragement helps no one at two in the afternoon outside room 412.

Go early in the day when you can, before the tests and the exhaustion. Wash your hands at the door so they can see you do it. Do not sit on the bed. The bed is the one square of territory the patient still controls, and a body is fighting for every inch of control it has left. Pull a chair. Get below their eye line if you can, so they are not looking up at one more authority who has come to do something to them.

Stay short. Twenty minutes is a gift. Forty minutes is a burden dressed as devotion.

Do not narrate their illness back to them. They have heard the doctors. They do not need you to explain the diagnosis or to tell them about your aunt who had the same thing and either died or did not, both of which are the wrong story. Ask one honest question and then be quiet long enough for the answer to come. How are you, really. And then wait. The silence will be uncomfortable for you and necessary for them. When you pray, pray short and pray true. Do not use the prayer to preach a sermon you could not fit into Sunday. Name the fear out loud, because a fear named in the presence of God is a fear that has been handed to someone stronger. Then go, before you wear them out. The visit is for them. It was never for you.

sections.title: At the Bed Where Someone Is Dying
sections.body:
There will come a day, and not rarely, when you are called to the room where a person is leaving. The breathing has changed. The family is gathered or scattered or fighting in the hallway. You are the one they sent for, and you have no idea what you are doing, and that feeling never fully goes away. Good. The day it stops frightening you is the day you should stop going.

You are not there to fix it. There is nothing to fix. There is only someone to accompany to the edge of a country you cannot enter with them.

So do the old things, because the old things hold when nothing else will. Read the twenty-third Psalm slowly, even if the person seems past hearing, because hearing is the last sense to go and the cadence of those words was carved into them before they could read. Say the Lord's Prayer and let the family join the parts their childhood remembers. Tell the dying person it is all right to go, if the family can bear it, because sometimes a person holds on out of fear that those they love cannot release them. Tell them they are not alone. Tell them the Lord who walked through his own death is walking with them now. Then be quiet and let the room be holy. I have stood in that room and felt utterly useless. I have learned that useless, in that room, is the wrong word. The word is faithful. You came. You stayed. You did not run from the one thing every one of us will face.

sections.title: The Discipline of Going
sections.body:
You will not feel like it. That is not a reason. Feelings make a poor foreman for the unglamorous work, and the unglamorous work is most of the work. So build it into the week the way you build in study, or it will be the first thing crowded out by the urgent and the visible.

Keep a list. Know who is sick, who is shut in, who has gone quiet. The quiet ones are often the drowning ones.

Go before the crisis when you can, because the relationship you build over ordinary coffee is the relationship that will hold weight when the diagnosis comes. The pastor who only appears when someone is dying is a stranger at the worst possible moment. Do not measure this work by its yield. It has no yield you can count. You will pour hours into people who leave the church, people who never thank you, people who forget you came. Pour anyway. The Shepherd left the ninety-nine for the one, and the one was not grateful, and the one did not grow the flock, and the Shepherd went anyway.

This is the work. It will not make you famous. It will make you a pastor. Go.
